title: Her husband's timidity and selling Alabama Bound for $500
summary: He was timid, not a salesman, and sold his piece Alabama Bound to Kramer for $500.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Mm-hmm. I see. Well, that's a lot of fun. Well, anyway, when he quit playing in theaters and things, did he play his own pieces at home? When he'd entertain people at the church, would he play his own pieces? No. That's funny. He was timid, you say.

Well, I think my husband, he was a soft-voiced kind of man and he was timid. I can't think of any better word to describe. And how you know some people are the salesman type. Yeah. Well, he's just not. He was just opposite to that. So, I think that's the reason, even in the days that these things were written, that he wasn't a hustler. Yeah. He didn't get tied up with people who were, you know, that could push these things.
I really find it curious. You said he didn't get a lot of money out of writing pieces like I'm Alabama-bound.
No, he told me he sold it to Kramer for $500. Mm-hmm. That was it.
Well, I guess $500 was more money than those days.
Yes. Oh, yes. It would be like $1,500 maybe. Mm-hmm. But he didn't really get the money like anybody now can make a record.
You know, and get a fortune, make a fortune out of it.
If they've got the right royalty agreement and everything. Yeah. And it sells. Of course, it takes a lot of promotion. You have to have that salesman's year.
But I don't think anybody really made these Northrop and different ones. Mm-hmm. I think they really made their money in latter years if they're still living.
